Buyers of Rigetti Computing (RGTI) stock may be betting on the company's ability to sell whole quantum computers. Rigetti already fills orders for its Novera systems, which customers install on site, even though quantum computing can look like a research field that is years away from real sales. Yet the stock lost 74.9% over the past year while the S&P 500 returned 17.1%, and that is the contradiction. So how much is Rigetti actually selling?

Rigetti's Quarterly Revenue Nearly Tripled On Novera Systems

Rigetti recorded $5.14 million in revenue during the second quarter of fiscal 2026, a 185.3% increase from a year earlier. Management said on the August 6, 2026 call that on-premises Novera sales provided the increase, as orders announced earlier turned into revenue.

The company still needs to convert one order into revenue. Rigetti is building a 108-qubit system for C-DAC in India under an $8.4 million order, and management expects to book that revenue in the fourth quarter of 2026. This single order equals about 63% of the $13.4 million in revenue Rigetti generated over the four quarters to June.

Demand is also spreading. Management reported more demand for Novera systems from national labs and universities, while the first two 9-qubit systems Rigetti delivered in 2026 both went to commercial organizations.

Rigetti Still Loses Far More Than It Sells

Anyone holding the stock faces the worry that Rigetti spends far more than it sells. The company posted an operating loss of $97.2 million over the four quarters to June, an amount more than seven times its revenue.

Rigetti does keep more of each sale than it did previously. Gross margin reached 42.6% in the June quarter, against 31.4% a year earlier. Yet the operating loss for the quarter still grew, climbing to $28.1 million from $19.9 million.

The share price appears to include a lot of sales Rigetti has not made yet, trading at 291 times sales against 3.1 times for the S&P 500. Rigetti also held $394 million in cash and short-term investments at the end of June, against $7.7 million of debt. This cash alone amounts to about $1.18 for each share, measured against a share price of $11.66, the lowest close of the past year.

What Could Go Wrong With Rigetti's Machine Sales?

Rigetti's sales can slip from one quarter to the next, since management says results follow the timing of large system contracts. Revenue in the fourth quarter of 2025 fell 17.9% from a year earlier to $1.87 million. The C-DAC revenue also comes only after the system is installed in India and passes acceptance testing.

title: PayPal, Nike and Zoom top the list of market-value losers since 2021

PayPal, Nike and Zoom top the list of market-value losers since 2021
CFO.com · Michael M. Santiago / Staff via Getty Images

This story was originally published on CFO.com. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO.com newsletter.

Back in the good old days, buying blue-chip stocks with iron-solid brand names, like IBM and General Motors, was thought to be the next safest investment strategy after loading up on U.S. Treasuries.

That's far from the case in the topsy-turvy 2020s, as demonstrated by a new report from investment research platform BestBrokers. The message for CFOs: Watch out; your brand may not be as unassailable as you thought.

Almost anyone who doesn't regularly pay attention to stock market news would likely be surprised to learn that the shares of familiar, highly successful companies like PayPal, Nike and Zoom have plummeted in recent years.

Leaving out companies with major acquisitions, mergers and other significant structural changes, plus those that executed major forward stock splits, BestBrokers identified 172 companies worldwide that saw large chunks of their market value wiped out since 2021.

For the hardest-hit stocks, the losses appear almost surreal. A $1,000 investment in PayPal at the close of business on Aug. 13, 2021, had declined in value to $200.21 by Sept. 25, 2026.

Similarly, $1,000 worth of shares in Nike and Zoom collapsed during the same time frame to $208.22 and $252.53, respectively. Other U.S. companies among the 20 worst market performers across the five-year period include Block (formerly Square), Estée Lauder, Crown Castle, Zoetis, Adobe, Comcast, Coupang and Infosys.

"These results serve as a reminder that a famous name, a once-dominant position or a history of success is no guarantee of lasting investor confidence," BestBrokers wrote.

Why did the market values of these companies crash so spectacularly? The answers vary widely.

In PayPal's case, the culprit was not a collapse in revenue or payments activity. Rather, as online shopping surged during the Covid lockdowns, "investors priced in years of rapid growth," the report noted. "When consumers returned to physical stores, that momentum faded — and competition from Apple Pay, Google Pay, Stripe and other payment providers intensified."

While tougher competition was a factor for Nike too, value-damaging issues included its product mix, the online direct-to-consumer model it turned to, and heavy reliance on promotions. All of these have eroded Nike's appeal and premium brand image, slowing customer demand and revenue, BestBrokers said in the report.

Block, for its part, struggled as the digital payments landscape fractured into competing apps, while Estée Lauder failed to recover from a prolonged slowdown in travel and weak sales in China, according to the report. For Adobe, even though it's building AI into its products, "the evidence that these tools can generate substantial new revenue and defend subscription pricing is probably not clear enough," according to the report.

International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 21, 2026, after the market closes.

Analysts expect earnings per share of $2.86, compared with $2.65 a year earlier. Revenue is projected to reach $16.82 billion, up from $16.33 billion.

Analyst Ratings And Price Forecasts

The stock carries a Buy rating, with an average price target of $259.76. Recent analyst actions include:

Morgan Stanley: Equal-Weight; raised its price target to $238.00 (Oct. 15).

RBC Capital: Outperform; maintained its price target at $270.00 (Oct. 13).

Truist Securities: Initiated coverage with a Hold rating and a $240.00 price target (Oct. 9).

Major AI Partnerships And Product Developments

In recent months, IBM announced several partnerships, product launches and deployments aimed at expanding its AI capabilities and enterprise offerings.

IBM formed a strategic partnership with OpenAI to help companies deploy artificial intelligence across core business operations while strengthening cybersecurity.

IBM announced a self-hosted deployment option for IBM Bob, its agentic software development platform, designed to help enterprises strengthen AI sovereignty and governance.

The company disclosed a research collaboration with Siemens Energy AG (OTC:SMERY) to advance its next-generation nanostack semiconductor architecture, targeting AI and other emerging technologies over the coming decade.

IBM is also expanding its AI capabilities through a $240 million, multiyear agreement with Together AI.

IBM Edge Scorecard: Quality Strength vs Value Weakness

Momentum: Neutral (Score: 37.77) — The stock's recent push is improving, but it's not showing sustained leadership versus the broader market.

Quality: Strong (Score: 81.33) — IBM screens well on quality metrics, which can help support the stock during choppier tape.

Value: Weak (Score: 25.29) — Valuation looks less compelling on this model, so buyers may want clearer trend confirmation before paying up.

Growth: Neutral (Score: 41.15) — Growth factors are middling, keeping the story more execution-driven than hyper-growth.

The Verdict: International Business Machines's Benzinga Edge signal reveals a quality-led profile with only moderate momentum and growth support. Is IonQ Stock A Buy Today, Down By Half In A Year?

IonQ (IONQ) stock lost 50.3% over the past year, while the S&P 500 returned 17.1%. The business moved in the opposite direction, with management calling the second quarter of 2026 its fifth consecutive quarter of record results. Yet the company still loses far more money than it brings in. So how much growth does a buyer get for today's price?

What Buyers Pay For IonQ's Sales Growth

A buyer pays 46.6 times IonQ's sales over the past twelve months, compared with 3.1 times for the S&P 500. Because the company reported a loss, a price-to-earnings ratio is not meaningful for IonQ.

For that price, the buyer gets very fast growth. IonQ's revenue reached $246 million in the twelve months ended June 30, 2026, climbing 370.6% from a year earlier. Over the last three twelve-month periods, S&P 500 revenue growth averaged 5.9%. IonQ bought part of that growth. Management said organic revenue, which excludes acquired businesses, rose 132% in the second quarter of 2026, against 286.8% growth in total revenue.

The signed work behind those sales has also grown, and that may be what stock buyers are betting on. IonQ ended the second quarter with $485 million of remaining performance obligations, representing revenue under contract that it has not yet delivered. That figure was up from $122 million a year earlier.

Can IonQ Keep Funding Big Operating Losses?

So far IonQ can, because it has cash on hand and continues to raise more. Its operating loss over the twelve months ended June 30 equaled 408.2% of its revenue, while the S&P 500 earned an operating margin of 18.5%. At June 30, IonQ held $2.1 billion in cash and short-term investments, compared with $54.5 million of debt.

IonQ priced a $2.0 billion equity offering on October 14, and management said the money will accelerate the commercialization of its quantum platform. New shares also pay for its acquisitions. On October 12, IonQ agreed to buy the cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion. Paying in stock will expand the share count, meaning existing investors will face ownership dilution once that transaction closes.

What To Watch In IonQ's November Report

IonQ's next quarterly report is expected on or around November 11, 2026. It will be the company's first report covering a quarter in which it owned SkyWater, which IonQ bought for $1.8 billion in the week before its August 5 call. On that August 5 call, management raised standalone 2026 guidance to between $280 million and $290 million before following up at its September 8 Investor Day with a combined target of $450 million to $460 million. How smoothly SkyWater integrates to meet that combined revenue target will be the key operational metric to watch in November.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock trades at 153.2 times its earnings over the past twelve months, compared with 23.0 for the S&P 500. Buyers paying that price appear to be betting on sustained expansion. During an August 3 call, management pointed to a single customer segment outpacing the rest of the business and raised its 2026 forecast for that group. Who are those customers, and how much are they already buying?

Palantir's American Business Customers Are Buying Fastest

Those customers are American companies. Palantir generated $764 million in U.S. commercial revenue during the second quarter of fiscal 2026, a 149% increase from a year earlier. Sales to the U.S. government, the company's other major domestic market, grew 90% over the same period, meaning domestic corporate sales are expanding faster than sales to the government.

The client roster is expanding alongside those sales, though at a slower pace. Palantir finished the quarter with 653 U.S. commercial customers. That total is up 35% from a year earlier, suggesting individual clients are spending more on average.

Newly signed contracts reflect a similar trend. U.S. commercial bookings, which track the total value of agreements signed during the quarter, climbed 153% from a year earlier to a record $2.132 billion. That figure is almost three times the U.S. commercial revenue generated over the same three months. However, bookings count the full value of contracts, and management noted that some of these deals extend for three years.

How Big Could Palantir's Sales To American Companies Get?

Management expects U.S. commercial revenue to exceed $3.424 billion in 2026, representing growth of at least 134%. That target would account for about 42% of the $8.15 billion to $8.158 billion in total revenue the company forecast for the year. While both figures are projections rather than reported results, they demonstrate that sales to American companies have evolved past being a side business for Palantir.

The share price appears to assume a good deal of that growth already. Palantir trades at 75.1 times its sales over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 trades at 3.1 times. The stock delivered a 54.6% return from July 22 to October 20, 2026, compared with 3.1% for the index. On October 20, shares closed 7.9% below their highest close of the past year.
